lead: This unit explains what the Internet of Things is, how a thing is built and described, and how its parts communicate and fit into an architecture. You will learn to separate physical design from logical design, compare IoT with M2M, name the enabling technologies and challenges, and read the market value chain. After it you can label an IoT system's blocks, choose a communication model, and sketch a layered architecture for an exam answer.
about: The unit covers the foundations of IoT: what it is, how a thing is built, what functions it performs, how its parts communicate, and how those parts are arranged in layers. Chapter 1.1 defines IoT and its evolution. 1.2 moves to physical devices and components. 1.3 turns the hardware into logical functional blocks. 1.4 explains communication models and APIs, and 1.5 places them in layered architectures. 1.6 lists enabling technologies, 1.7 compares IoT with M2M, and 1.8 examines challenges and impact. 1.9 closes with value chains and market perspective. Each chapter adds one view of the same system so exam answers can move from definition to architecture to business.

chapters.idea: IoT is a network of identifiable physical things that sense, act and exchange data over networks to deliver services with little or no direct human control.
chapters.depth: Cover definition, the words thing and internet, and characteristics: connectivity, identity, sensing, actuation, intelligence, energy limit, heterogeneity and dynamic operation. Trace evolution from early M2M and RFID through wireless sensor networks, IP and cloud, IoT platforms, and edge and AI. Some syllabi call this definition and characteristics of IoT, foundations, or evolution. Mention impact only in one line; details come in 1.8.

figure.title: Evolution of IoT
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain from early machine-to-machine links through RFID, wireless sensor networks, IP and cloud, IoT platforms, to edge and AI.

chapters.example: A city installs 2,000 smart water meters. Each meter sends 24 readings per day and each reading is 40 bytes. Find the raw data per day in kB, taking 1 kB = 1000 bytes. Answer: 2,000 × 24 × 40 = 1,920,000 bytes = 1,920 kB per day.
chapters.trap: Do not define IoT as only internet-connected sensors. The service and the action on the physical world are part of the definition.
chapters.leave: Detailed sensor physics, radio protocols, cloud platforms, security mechanisms and application case studies go to Units 2–6.

chapters.idea: The physical design names the actual things and devices and the parts inside them: sensors, actuators, a control unit, a communication module and a power source.
chapters.depth: Separate physical design from logical design. Describe a thing as a physical object with identity, and a device as its engineering package. Cover components: control unit such as a microcontroller or single-board computer, sensors, actuators, communication module, and power source such as battery, mains or energy harvesting. Use Arduino, Raspberry Pi and ESP8266 only as example control units. Mention RFID tags and gateways. Some syllabi call this things in IoT, components in IoT, or physical design. Keep sensor types and board details for Units 2 and 4.

figure.aria: A box tree with IoT device at the root and five parts below it: sensors, actuators, control unit, communication module and power source.

chapters.example: A soil-moisture node uses a 3.7 V, 2,000 mAh battery. Sleep current is 20 µA, and active current is 30 mA for 2 s every 1 hour. Estimate average current and battery life, ignoring conversion loss. Answer: average current = (30 mA × 2 s + 0.02 mA × 3598 s) ÷ 3600 s = 0.0367 mA. Life = 2000 mAh ÷ 0.0367 mA ≈ 54,500 h ≈ 6.2 years.
chapters.trap: Do not confuse physical design with logical design. A sensor is one component, not the whole IoT system.
chapters.leave: Sensor characteristics and actuator types go to Unit 2; board programming and interfacing go to Unit 4; radio standards go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The logical design describes what functions an IoT system performs, independent of which hardware implements them.
chapters.depth: List functional blocks: identification, sensing, actuation, communication, processing, services, management and security. Show the data path from a thing to a service. Explain that identification gives names or addresses, sensing collects state, processing makes decisions, communication moves data, and services present useful output. Management covers configuration and faults; security cuts across all blocks. Some syllabi call this logical design, functional view, or IoT functional blocks. Keep protocols and hardware out of the block list.

figure.title: Logical functional blocks
figure.aria: A downward flow from identification to sensing, processing, communication and services, with management and security as dashed control blocks.

chapters.example: A cold-chain van has 6 temperature sensors, 1 GPS unit and 2 door sensors. Every sensor produces one data item every 5 minutes. Find the number of data items per day. Answer: total sensors = 6 + 1 + 2 = 9. Samples per day = 24 × 60 ÷ 5 = 288. Data items = 9 × 288 = 2,592 per day.
chapters.trap: Do not list hardware when asked for functional blocks. Functions are verbs such as identify, sense, process, communicate, manage and secure.
chapters.leave: Detailed protocols go to Unit 3; cloud processing and security mechanisms go to Unit 5; actuator hardware goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: IoT systems exchange data through a few interaction patterns, and APIs expose those patterns to programs.
chapters.depth: Define communication model and API, meaning application programming interface. Cover request-response, publish-subscribe, push-pull and exclusive pair. Explain broker, topic and decoupling for publish-subscribe. Cover REST-style APIs over HTTP with GET, PUT, POST and DELETE, plus WebSocket for full-duplex links. Name MQTT and CoAP only as examples of the models. Some syllabi call this IoT communication models and IoT communication APIs. Do not teach packet headers or QoS details here.

figure.aria: A sequence diagram of a request-response API call: the client asks the API server, the server reads the device, and the value returns to the client.

chapters.example: A REST API is polled by 50 clients every 10 s. Each request is 300 bytes and each response is 500 bytes. Find traffic per hour in MB, taking 1 MB = 10^6 bytes. Answer: per client per poll = 300 + 500 = 800 bytes. Per hour there are 3600 ÷ 10 = 360 polls. Traffic = 50 × 800 × 360 = 14,400,000 bytes = 14.4 MB per hour.
chapters.trap: Do not call MQTT request-response. MQTT is publish-subscribe through a broker. An API is an interface, not a radio protocol.
chapters.leave: MQTT QoS, CoAP details, HTTP packet formats, 6LoWPAN, LoRaWAN and NB-IoT go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An IoT architecture is a set of layers or tiers that organises where data is sensed, moved, processed and used.
chapters.depth: Explain why architecture is needed. Cover the 3-layer model: perception, network and application. Cover the 5-layer model: perception, transport, processing, application and business. Cover the seven-level IoT World Forum reference model from physical devices and controllers up to collaboration and processes, with management and security as cross-cutting concerns. Include edge-fog-cloud placement and design principles: scalability, modularity, interoperability, security, privacy, reliability, energy efficiency and open standards. Some syllabi call this architectural overview, building an architecture, or layered reference model. Only a few universities teach the seven-level model in detail; keep the level names clear.

figure.aria: A seven-level stack from physical devices and connectivity through edge computing, data accumulation, data abstraction and application to collaboration, with business value at the top.

chapters.example: A 3-layer design has 4,000 sensors. Each sensor sends 1 packet per minute. The network layer aggregates 20 packets into one uplink. Find the uplinks per minute. Answer: 4,000 ÷ 20 = 200 uplinks per minute.
chapters.trap: Do not mix the layer names of the 3-layer and 5-layer models. Perception or sensing is the bottom layer, and business is the top only in the 5-layer model.
chapters.leave: Cloud and fog implementation goes to Unit 5; the NB-IoT protocol stack goes to Unit 3; domain applications go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: IoT is possible because several mature technologies combine: sensing, embedded computing, wireless networks, cloud, big data and analytics.
chapters.depth: Cover enabling technologies one by one: RFID and identification, wireless sensor networks, embedded systems and microcontrollers, communication protocols and wireless links such as IEEE 802.15.4, ZigBee, Bluetooth and BLE, Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN and NB-IoT, mobile Internet and 4G/5G, cloud computing, big data analytics, edge and fog computing. Give one line on LTE history and 5G features: enhanced mobile broadband, massive machine-type communication and ultra-reliable low-latency communication. Describe NB-IoT as narrowband, licensed-spectrum, low-power wide-area with massive low-throughput devices, long battery life, deep coverage and low device cost. Only a few universities teach the detailed NB-IoT protocol stack here; it belongs to Unit 3.

figure.aria: A graph with IoT at the centre connected to sensors, embedded systems, networks, cloud, analytics, RFID, and 5G and NB-IoT.

chapters.example: A narrowband sensor sends 512 bytes every 30 minutes, and there are 10,000 such devices. Find total uplink data per day in MB, taking 1 MB = 10^6 bytes. Answer: samples per device per day = 24 × 60 ÷ 30 = 48. Data per device = 512 × 48 = 24,576 bytes. Total = 10,000 × 24,576 = 245,760,000 bytes = 245.76 MB per day.
chapters.trap: Do not treat NB-IoT as high-speed 5G broadband. NB-IoT is for massive numbers of low-throughput devices with long battery life.
chapters.leave: Radio standards and protocol stacks go to Unit 3; cloud platforms and analytics go to Unit 5; board details go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: M2M connects machines directly for monitoring and control, while IoT adds internet-scale addressing, cloud services, analytics and human-facing applications.
chapters.depth: Define M2M and IoT. Compare communication path, scale, standards, protocols, data use, ownership and typical examples. M2M is often point-to-point, proprietary and limited to monitoring. IoT is many-to-many, uses IP or cloud platforms, supports analytics and services, and often has open standards. Mention that M2M value chains are covered in 1.9. Some syllabi call this machine-to-machine communication or IoT versus M2M. Avoid treating M2M as an old name for exactly the same system.

figure.aria: A two-set Venn diagram showing M2M with direct links and monitoring, IoT with cloud, analytics and apps, and shared devices, sensors and connectivity in the overlap.

chapters.example: A fleet has 800 trucks. An M2M SIM sends 1 SMS of 140 bytes every hour. An IoT version sends 20 kB every hour through a cloud platform. Compare daily data per truck and total for the fleet. Answer: M2M per truck per day = 140 × 24 = 3,360 bytes = 3.36 kB. M2M total = 800 × 3.36 kB = 2,688 kB = 2.69 MB. IoT per truck per day = 20 × 24 = 480 kB. IoT total = 800 × 480 kB = 384,000 kB = 384 MB.
chapters.trap: Do not say M2M is simply a subset of IoT. M2M is an earlier, narrower form and is not always internet-connected.
chapters.leave: M2M value chains and industrial structure go to 1.9; detailed protocols go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: IoT creates technical, business and social issues, and its impact is both positive and negative.
chapters.depth: Cover technical challenges: scale, heterogeneity, interoperability, energy, connectivity, latency, reliability, data volume, identification and addressing. Cover security and privacy: authentication, authorization, confidentiality, integrity, availability, updates, physical access and trust. Cover business issues such as cost, return on investment and skills, and social issues such as surveillance, e-waste, digital divide and safety. Explain impact: efficiency, safety and new services, balanced against dependence and job change. Some syllabi call this challenges and issues or impact of IoT.

figure.aria: A tree of IoT challenges grouped under technical, security, business and society, each with example issues below.

chapters.example: A building has 5,000 sensors. Each firmware update is 250 kB. The gateway updates 50 devices at a time at 2 Mbps. Find the time for one batch and for all batches, ignoring overhead. Answer: one batch data = 50 × 250 kB = 12,500 kB. At 2 Mbps = 2,000,000 bits/s = 250,000 bytes/s = 250 kB/s. One batch time = 12,500 ÷ 250 = 50 s. Number of batches = 5,000 ÷ 50 = 100. Total time = 100 × 50 = 5,000 s = 83.3 min ≈ 1.39 h.
chapters.trap: Do not reduce IoT security to encryption only. Identity, firmware updates, physical access and privacy are also part of the issue.
chapters.leave: Detailed security mechanisms and privacy law go to Unit 5; application-specific risks go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: IoT value is created across a chain of suppliers, and market analysis asks where value and revenue sit in that chain.
chapters.depth: Cover M2M value chains and IoT value chains. Name roles: component and chip makers, device makers, network operators, platform providers, system integrators, application and service providers, and end users. Explain the emerging industrial structure and why partnerships and standards matter. Cover market perspective: segments, business models such as subscription and pay-per-use, everything as a service or XaaS, business processes, analytics and knowledge management. Some syllabi call this market perspective of IoT based systems or emerging industrial structure. Only a few universities teach detailed industrial-structure models; keep those short.

figure.title: IoT value chain
figure.aria: A left-to-right value chain from component makers through device makers, network operators and platform providers to application providers and end users.

chapters.example: A smart-meter service charges ₹80 per meter per month for 25,000 meters. Platform cost is ₹5,00,000 per month, and SIM and connectivity cost is ₹15 per meter per month. Find monthly revenue, total cost and margin. Answer: revenue = 25,000 × ₹80 = ₹20,00,000. Connectivity cost = 25,000 × ₹15 = ₹3,75,000. Total cost = ₹3,75,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹8,75,000. Margin = ₹20,00,000 − ₹8,75,000 = ₹11,25,000, which is 56.25% of revenue.
chapters.trap: Do not equate the value chain with hardware manufacturing only. Connectivity, platforms, data and services also carry value.
chapters.leave: Cloud platform details go to Unit 5; application case studies go to Unit 6; detailed business strategy is beyond this unit.
